weeks.title: 1 to 3 weeks pregnant: conception, symptoms and first steps
weeks.description: In weeks 1 and 2 there is no baby yet: the count starts at your last period. When ovulation, fertilisation and implantation happen, and when to test.
weeks.quickAnswer: Weeks 1 to 3 are the start of the 1st month and the 1st trimester, but for the first two there is no baby yet. Pregnancy is counted from the first day of your last period, and conception does not usually happen until around the end of week 2. In week 3 the fertilised egg travels to the womb. There is no size or weight to measure yet, and a pregnancy test only becomes reliable once your period is late.

weeks.title: 4 weeks pregnant: a 2 mm embryo, symptoms and first steps
weeks.description: At 4 weeks the embryo is about 2 mm long and has just implanted in the womb. When a test turns positive, early symptoms and how antenatal care starts.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 4 weeks you are at the end of the 1st month and in the 1st trimester. The embryo is about 2 mm long, roughly the size of a poppy seed, and has just implanted in the wall of the womb. This is the week your period is late and a pregnancy test usually turns positive.

weeks.title: 5 weeks pregnant: baby size, symptoms and first steps
weeks.description: At 5 weeks the embryo is about 2 mm long and the heart starts to beat. Early pregnancy symptoms, what a scan can show and when to book antenatal care.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 5 weeks you are at the start of the 2nd month and in the 1st trimester. The embryo is about 2 mm long, the size of a sesame seed, and the heart starts to form and to beat around now. This is the week many women find out they are pregnant, and the practical next step is booking your first antenatal appointment.

weeks.title: 6 weeks pregnant: baby size, symptoms and first appointments
weeks.description: At 6 weeks the embryo is about 6 mm long and the heartbeat can sometimes be seen on a scan. Nausea, mild cramps, what needs checking and how to start care.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 6 weeks you are in the 2nd month and the 1st trimester. The embryo is about 6 mm from head to bottom, roughly the size of a lentil, and the buds of the arms and legs are starting to show. For many women this is the week nausea settles in, and it is a good time to arrange your first appointment.

weeks.title: 7 weeks pregnant: baby size, symptoms and your first appointment
weeks.description: At 7 weeks the embryo is about 10 mm long and the brain is growing fast. Nausea, mild cramps, booking your first appointment and avoiding toxoplasmosis.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 7 weeks you are in the 2nd month and the 1st trimester. The embryo is about 10 mm long from head to bottom, roughly the size of a blueberry, and the brain is growing faster than the rest of the body. For many women this is when nausea gets worse, and it is the week to arrange your first antenatal appointment if you have not done so yet.

weeks.title: 36 weeks pregnant: baby size, symptoms and prenatal care
weeks.description: At 36 weeks your baby is about 47.4 cm long and weighs about 2.7 kg. Is it still preterm, why the baby drops into your pelvis, and what changes in your care.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 36 weeks you are starting the 9th month, in the third trimester. Your baby is about 47.4 cm long from head to heel and weighs about 2.7 kg, roughly the size of a romaine lettuce. Their lungs are probably ready to breathe outside the womb, but a birth this week still counts as preterm. Many babies have already moved head down, and some drop into the pelvis.

weeks.title: 37 weeks pregnant: early term, signs of labour and antenatal care
weeks.description: At 37 weeks your baby is about 48.6 cm long and weighs about 3 kg. What early term means, the signs that labour is starting and when to call your unit.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 37 weeks you are in the 9th month, in the third trimester. Your baby is about 48.6 cm long from head to heel and weighs about 3 kg, roughly the size of a bunch of Swiss chard. From this week a birth is no longer counted as premature, so the focus shifts to recognising the signs of labour.

weeks.title: 38 weeks pregnant: baby size, symptoms and prenatal care
weeks.description: At 38 weeks your baby is about 49.8 cm long and weighs about 3.2 kg. Signs that labour is near, common symptoms and what to do this week.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 38 weeks you are in the 9th month, in the third trimester, and your baby is early term, so no longer preterm if born now. Your baby is about 49.8 cm long from head to heel and weighs about 3.2 kg, roughly the length of a leek. Meconium, which will be the first poo, is building up in the bowel, and your body may start showing signs that the birth is near.

weeks.title: 39 weeks pregnant: baby size, labour signs and prenatal care
weeks.description: At 39 weeks you reach full term and your baby weighs about 3.4 kg. Signs labour is starting, the mucus plug, and when to go to hospital.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 39 weeks you are in the 9th month, at the end of the third trimester, and your pregnancy has reached what is called full term. Your baby is about 50.7 cm long from head to heel and weighs about 3.4 kg, roughly the size of a small watermelon. Labour could start any day, so this is the week to know the signs and when to head to hospital.

weeks.title: 40 weeks pregnant: due date, labour signs and prenatal care
weeks.description: At 40 weeks the baby is about 51.2 cm long and weighs about 3.6 kg. What happens if labour doesn't start, the signs of labour and when to go in.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 40 weeks you are at the end of the 9th month and the third trimester, in your due-date week. The baby is about 51.2 cm from head to heel and weighs about 3.6 kg, roughly the size of a pumpkin. Your baby is full term, and reaching this week with no sign of labour is common: only about 1 in 20 babies is born on the due date itself.

weeks.title: 41 and 42 weeks pregnant: past your due date, now what?
weeks.description: At 41 weeks a pregnancy is late term and at 42 weeks it is post-term. How monitoring changes, when induction comes up and the signs of labour.
weeks.quickAnswer: At 41 weeks your pregnancy has gone past the due date and is called late term. From 42 full weeks it is called post-term. Your baby is usually ready to be born and tends to weigh between 3 and 4 kg. From here on, antenatal care gets closer, with more checks on the baby's wellbeing and a conversation with your care team about waiting or having labour induced.
